card.intuition: Splitting a single logical database across many physical database nodes by partitioning rows, usually by a shard key. Each shard holds a subset of the data and handles its own reads and writes in parallel, letting the system scale beyond a single machine's storage and throughput limits.
card.analogy: Dividing a city's phone book into volumes by first-letter ranges: looking up "Anderson" only requires opening the A volume instead of flipping through one giant book. Splitting the work across volumes means several people can search at once.
card.time_complexity: O(log n) per-shard lookups where n is the rows per shard; routing adds O(1) hash or O(log N) range lookup to find the target shard.
card.space_complexity: Total storage is distributed across S shards; each shard holds roughly 1/S of the data, but hot keys can skew utilization.
when_to_use: Scaling write throughput or storage beyond what a single database instance can handle
Partitioning by a natural key (user_id, tenant_id, region) so related rows stay colocated
Isolating faults: one shard failing does not take down the entire dataset
gotchas: Querying across shards is expensive: joins, aggregations, and transactions spanning shards get complex
Choosing a poor shard key or an uneven distribution causes hotspot shards; resharing afterward is painful
Data is not inherently distributed — a hash on a monotonic ID can concentrate recent writes on one shard

steps.annotation: A request arrives carrying a shard key, usually a user or tenant id.
A router hashes the key to determine which shard owns that row, routing the query.
The request is served read-write from the owning shard; replicas add read redundancy.
Different keys land on different shards, so writes and reads are processed in parallel.
Cross-shard queries are forwarded to every shard and merged — the costly path to avoid.

exercise.prompt: A 10-node shard cluster can sustain 5,000 writes/second total. A hot product causes 2,500 writes/second to a single node. What is the maximum even per-node write rate the cluster can sustain if the load is perfectly balanced?
exercise.starter_code:
nodes = 10
peak_write_rate = 5000

per_node_even = peak_write_rate / nodes
# Result is ___ writes/second per node
hints: Evenly distributing means dividing the total capacity by the node count
exercise.test_code:
def check(ans):
    try: return int(ans) == 500
    except: return False
assert check("500")
